newsitem.title: USA: Clinton walks political tightrope on Cuba sanction.
newsitem.headline: Clinton walks political tightrope on Cuba sanction.

text.p: President Bill Clinton walked a political and diplomatic tightrope in the latest fight over sanctions on Cuba -- balancing his political needs with U.S. global interests.
In the end, his highwire journey took him to exactly where he wanted to go: back where he started.'

He announced on Friday that he was fully prepared to keep delaying a controversial provision in the so-called Helms-Burton law that has angered close allies, who say it interferes with the rights of their own citizens.

In effect his decision ended a risky political journey that took him from total opposition to the bill, to acceptance of it and, finally, to saying he would keep what he did not like from going into effect.
The tortuous debate over the sanctions coincided with a remarkable recovery of political fortunes for the president.

When he started the process, Clinton was facing a host of Republican challengers convinced they could oust him from the White House. After a remarkable comeback last year, he is now preparing to be sworn in later this month for a second term.

White House officials insist the decision had nothing to do with politics, and instead was driven by America's economic and foreign policy interests. Critics say it is yet another example of "Slick Willie" at his best.

One year ago in January, Clinton was opposed to the law being pushed by two Republican conservatives -- Sen. Jesse Helms of North Carolina and Representative Dan Burton of California, preferring other means to pressure communist Cuba.

By March, with his race for re-election in full gear, Clinton was signing the bill into law with great fanfare after Cuban MiG fighters had shot down two unarmed U.S. civilian aircraft over international waters -- killing anti-Castro Cubans living in Florida.

The incident generated enormous political pressure for the incumbent. Cuban-Americans pose a powerful force in voter-rich Florida and New Jersey, states Clinton had targeted as key to his re-election.

Senior campaign officials had said he particularly was "obsessed" with winning Florida, which he lost by a narrow margin in 1992 to then-President George Bush and which no Democratic presidential candidate had won in 20 years.
When Election Day came in November, Clinton won both Florida and New Jersey as he became the first Democrat to gain a second term since Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1936.

Clinton's main opposition to the Helms-Burton measure centred on the provision allowing U.S. citizens, including naturalised citizens from Cuba, to sue foreign companies doing business with property seized by Cuba's communist government after Fidel Castro took power in 1959.

Since enacted in March, the law has enraged Europeans, Canadians and Mexicans who accuse Washington of trying to impose its anti-Cuba trade sanctions on them. A number of countries have moved to enact laws to counter Helms-Burton and filed trade complaints to the World Trade Organisation.

"I would expect to continue suspending the right to file suit" as long as other nations join the call for democracy in Cuba, Clinton said, serving notice that he had no intention of letting the provision derail U.S. relations with its partners.
His decision followed last month's declaration by European countries that they would press for democracy and human rights in Cuba.

A Republican congressional source involved in drafting the original legislation said of Clinton's decision: "We don't like it." But he noted that "the law is still on the books" and said: "We'll just have to make sure the right president is elected next time."
